_readme.covers: Units 11-15. Rated progressions for the chords introduced in this range: supertonic and subdominant seventh chords in all inversions, applied dominants and tonicization, and the passing motion IV6 -> I6 within an expanded tonic.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord. Empty list = applies only to the first chord.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'V' matches any inversion of V.
matching.figured: A numeral with a figure like 'V65' matches only that inversion.
matching.applied: Applied dominants are written with a slash, e.g. 'V/V' or 'V7/V'.
matching.case: In minor keys the analyzer emits uppercase VII for the natural (modal) subtonic and lowercase vii for the raised (harmonic-minor) leading tone. Both forms are listed where a rule is intended to cover the seventh degree in either spelling.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Applied dominant of V resolving to V. Tonicizes the dominant — the strongest way to intensify a cadential approach without leaving the home key.
Applied dominant of ii resolving to ii. Prepares the predominant area with a strong local tonicization.
Applied dominant of vi resolving to vi. Prepares a deceptive-sounding arrival or a tonicization of the relative minor.
Applied dominant of iii resolving to iii. iii is the weakest diatonic goal, so this tonicization rarely stands on its own.

Applied dominant of the seventh degree. In a minor key the target is the natural subtonic (VII, a major triad on the modal 7th), which makes the resolution a modal cadence rather than a functional one.
Applied dominant of VII continuing on to the actual dominant. The tonicized target (VII) is bypassed in favour of the home dominant, producing a chromatic intensification of the cadential approach.
Introducing the applied dominant of V. This prepares a strong tonicization of the dominant.
Introducing the applied dominant of ii. Opens a tonicization of the supertonic, often at the start of a phrase.
Introducing the applied dominant of vi. Prepares a tonicization of the submediant or a deceptive arrival.
Introducing the applied dominant of IV. In major this is the tonic triad with a minor seventh (I7), which prepares a shift to the subdominant area.
Introducing the applied dominant of the mediant. Prepares a tonicization of III, common when a major-key passage moves toward its relative minor.
Introducing the applied dominant of the natural seventh. In a minor key this tonicizes the modal subtonic, preparing a modal cadence or a pivot toward the relative major.
IV6 to I6 with a stepwise descent in the bass (6 down to 3). Idiomatic passing motion within an expanded tonic, an alternative to vii°6 or V43.
IV6 to first-inversion dominant. Bass 6 to 7 with a stepwise ascent into the leading tone. Characteristic of the 6-7-8 bass line.
IV6 to vii°6. Bass 6 to 2 continues the expansion of tonic harmony before the cadence.
Root-position ii7 to the cadential 6/4. The 7th of ii is held over as the 4 of the 6/4, delaying its resolution to the 3 of V.
ii6/5 to the cadential 6/4. The dissonant 7th becomes the 4 of the cadential chord before resolving. One of the strongest pre-cadential approaches.
ii4/2 to I6. The chordal seventh in the bass must descend by step into V6, not continue into I6. This defeats the purpose of the inversion.
ii4/3 to root-position V. The bass leaps 6 to 5 while the seventh resolves. Workable, but the smoother resolution is to V6.
ii4/3 to tonic. The seventh of ii must resolve down into V; going directly to I leaves the dissonance unresolved.
ii4/2 to V6/5. The bass is the chordal seventh of ii and falls by step into the leading tone. V6/5 is the only idiomatic continuation.
IV7 to the cadential 6/4. The 7th of IV becomes the 4 of the 6/4. A frequent chromatic-flavoured approach to the cadence.
IV7 to tonic. The seventh of IV wants to resolve down into V, not leap to I. The direction is weak.
IV6/5 to V6/5 with a stepwise ascending bass (6 to 7). A characteristic 6-7-8 progression using two seventh chords.
IV6/5 to tonic. The seventh of IV resolves down into the root of I, and the bass steps 6 to 1. Acceptable in a non-cadential expansion.
